questions.prompt: SSIS packages run on two separate engines. Which one actually moves rows from a source to a destination, and which one decides the order tasks run in?
options: The data flow engine moves rows; the control flow engine manages task order, logging, and error handling across the package
The control flow engine moves rows; the data flow engine only decides which task runs next
Both engines move rows identically; the only difference is which tab of SSIS Designer they appear on
The runtime engine moves rows, while the data flow engine only logs what happened
questions.explain: SSIS packages are built on two separate engines: the control flow engine manages the order things happen in, which task runs first, and how errors and logging behave, while the data flow engine is a specialized engine dedicated entirely to moving and transforming rows between a source and a destination.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: installing the SQL Server Data Tools workload alone isn't enough to see the Integration Services Project template in the New Project dialog — you also need to install the separate ________ extension for your Visual Studio version.
questions.explain: SSDT itself is a Visual Studio workload, but Analysis Services, Integration Services, and Reporting Services each ship as their own separate Visual Studio extension. Without installing the Integration Services extension specifically, the Integration Services Project template simply won't appear, no matter how carefully SSDT was installed.

questions.prompt: Match each SSIS container concept to the file extension (or object) it actually corresponds to.
left: A package's complete, literal inventory of connection managers, variables, and executables
right: .sln — a container for one or more projects
.dtproj — lists the packages and configurations that belong to it
.dtsx — control flow, data flow, connection managers, and settings
The Package Explorer tab
questions.explain: A package is a .dtsx file holding control flow, data flow, connection managers, and settings. A project (.dtproj) lists the packages and configurations that belong to it. A solution (.sln) is a container for one or more projects. And the Package Explorer tab is where every one of a package's objects — connection managers, log providers, executables, variables — is listed as a literal tree.

questions.prompt: A developer stops the Windows "SQL Server Integration Services" service on their machine, then opens a package in SSDT and presses F5. What happens?
options: The package still opens, validates, and runs fine — the service only monitors packages stored the legacy way from SSMS, and isn't required to create, save, or run packages
SSDT refuses to open any package until the service is running again
The package runs, but every task silently fails because the service normally executes them
SSDT switches automatically to using the SSISDB catalog instead of running locally
questions.explain: The Integration Services Windows service is a legacy service that exists to monitor and manage packages stored in msdb or the file system, letting you start, stop, and list them from SSMS. Microsoft is explicit that the service is not required to create, save, or run Integration Services packages — you can design and execute a package with SSDT even with the service stopped.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about connection managers, per Lesson 5.
options: A connection manager is a design-time description of a connection; the actual physical connection is created at run time
A package can hold two separate OLE DB connection managers pointed at two different databases, each configured independently
A connection manager created in Solution Explorer at the project level is visible to every package in the project, shown with a (project) prefix
A package-level connection manager is automatically shared by every other package in the same project
The Connection Managers area only appears on the Control Flow tab — Data Flow and Event Handlers don't have one
questions.explain: A connection manager is a logical, design-time representation; the physical connection is created at run time. A package can hold multiple instances of the same connection manager type, each configured independently. A project-level connection manager, created in Solution Explorer, is shared by every package in the project and shown with a (project) prefix. A package-level connection manager, by contrast, exists only inside the package that created it — it is not shared automatically. And the Connection Managers area is docked along the bottom of the Control Flow, Data Flow, and Event Handlers tabs alike, not just Control Flow.

questions.prompt: An Execute SQL Task uses an OLE DB connection manager and runs this statement: SELECT * FROM Production.Product WHERE ProductID > ? AND ProductID < ?. Which Parameter Mapping setup correctly binds two input values to this statement?
options: Two Input parameters named 0 and 1, in the same order the two ? markers appear in the statement
Two Input parameters named @0 and @1, since OLE DB connections always prefix parameter names with @
Two Input parameters named Param1 and Param2, matched by name rather than position
One Input parameter named 0, since OLE DB only allows a single parameter per statement
Two Output parameters named 0 and 1, since Execute SQL Task parameters are always Output by default
Two Input parameters, with parameter order irrelevant since OLE DB binds by name
questions.explain: An OLE DB connection's parameter marker is ?, and its parameter name is an ordinal number — 0, 1, 2, and so on. The task binds parameters positionally, not by name, so the order of the parameter mappings must match the order the ? markers appear in the statement: the first ? maps to parameter 0, the second to parameter 1.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes the ADO connection type's naming convention — any name except an integer, like Param1 or Param2 — not OLE DB's. OLE DB (like EXCEL and ODBC) uses the ordinal ? marker matched positionally to parameters literally named 0, 1, 2, and getting the two connection types' marker conventions confused is exactly the mistake this lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: A package needs to run the same three tasks once for every file currently sitting in a folder, and the folder's file count changes from run to run. Which container is the right fit, and why?
options: A Foreach Loop container with the Foreach File enumerator — it runs once per item in a collection, and doesn't need to know the count in advance
A For Loop container, since EvalExpression can be set to check how many files are left
A Sequence Container, since it groups the three tasks so they only run once total
Either container works identically, since both just repeat whatever is inside them
questions.explain: The For Loop container answers "run this exactly this many times," evaluating a condition on every pass. The Foreach Loop container answers a different question — "run this once for every item in this collection" — without needing to know the count in advance. A folder of files with a changing count is exactly the Foreach File enumerator's job, not the For Loop's.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Execute Package Task, per Lesson 9.
options: With ReferenceType set to Project Reference, the child package must live in the same project as the parent, using the project deployment model
Setting ExecuteOutOfProcess to True means a crash in the child package is less likely to take the parent package's process down with it
A child package's logging details only reach the parent if the child has its own logging explicitly configured
ExecuteOutOfProcess set to False (the default) runs the child in its own separate process for safety
A transaction started in the parent package can extend into a child package, so work in both can be committed or rolled back together
questions.explain: Project Reference only works when the child lives in the same project under the project deployment model. ExecuteOutOfProcess set to True runs the child in its own process, so a child crash doesn't have to take the parent down with it. A transaction started in the parent can extend into the child so both can commit or roll back together. The child package always forwards its log details up to the parent regardless of whether the child has its own logging configured, and False — not True — is the default for ExecuteOutOfProcess, running the child in the parent's own process.

questions.prompt: Match each precedence constraint concept to what it actually controls, per Lesson 12.
left: Logical OR on multiple incoming constraints
right: The constrained executable runs regardless of whether the precedence executable succeeded or failed, as long as it finished
At least one incoming constraint must evaluate to True for the constrained executable to run
The constrained executable runs only if the precedence executable completed successfully
The constrained executable runs only if the precedence executable failed
questions.explain: Success (green, the default) runs the constrained executable only on a successful precedence executable. Failure (red) runs it only if the precedence executable failed. Completion (blue) runs it regardless of success or failure, as long as it finished. And when several constraints feed one executable, Logical OR means at least one of them has to evaluate to True, compared to Logical AND's requirement that every one of them does.

questions.prompt: A Foreach Loop container is being set up with the Foreach File enumerator to process every file in a folder. Put these configuration steps in the correct order.
items: On the Collection page, choose the Foreach File enumerator and point it at the target folder
Choose how to retrieve each file's name — name only, fully qualified path, or name and extension
On Variable Mappings, map the enumerator's current value to a package variable with Index 0
Use that variable in a property expression, such as a connection manager's ConnectionString, so downstream components see a different file on every pass
questions.explain: The Collection page is where you first pick the Foreach File enumerator and its folder, then choose how file names should be retrieved. Variable Mappings is what writes the enumerator's current value into a variable on every pass, with Index 0 since Foreach File only produces one value per iteration. Only after that mapping exists can a property expression elsewhere in the package — like a connection manager's ConnectionString — actually reference that variable to point at a different file each time.

questions.prompt: Of the three kinds of data flow components — sources, transformations, destinations — which one(s) have both an input and an output?
options: Transformations only — sources have no input, and destinations have no output into the data flow itself
Sources only, since they're where data enters the pipeline
Destinations only, since they're where the pipeline ends
All three have both an input and an output, since paths connect every component the same way
questions.explain: Sources have no input — only an output (and usually an error output) — because they're where data enters the data flow. Destinations have only an input (and usually an error output) — nothing flows out of them into the data flow. Transformations sit in the middle of the chain, so they're the only component type with both an input and an output.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Data Flow task's DefaultBufferSize property defaults to 10,485,760 bytes — ________ megabytes.
questions.explain: DefaultBufferSize's documented default is 10,485,760 bytes, which is 10 MB. The other buffer-size setting, DefaultMaxBufferRows, defaults to 10,000 rows per buffer.

questions.prompt: Match each data flow source/destination component to what it actually reads from or writes to, per Lesson 14.
right: An in-memory ADO recordset stored in a package variable, with no source counterpart
SSIS's own native binary format — no parsing, the fastest I/O there is
A delimited, fixed-width, or ragged-right text file
Any OLE DB-compliant relational database, using a table, view, or SQL command
questions.explain: OLE DB reads/writes any OLE DB-compliant database using a table, view, or SQL command. Flat File reads/writes a delimited, fixed-width, or ragged-right text file. Raw File reads/writes SSIS's own native binary format, with no parsing at all, making it the fastest possible I/O. Recordset Destination writes rows into an in-memory ADO recordset stored in a package variable, and has no source counterpart since its whole point is keeping data inside the package.

questions.prompt: An OLE DB Destination's Mappings page is left with one non-nullable destination column unmapped, and one nullable destination column unmapped. What happens when the package runs?
options: The load fails at run time because of the unmapped non-nullable column; the unmapped nullable column causes no problem at all
The load fails because of both unmapped columns — every destination column must be mapped
Both unmapped columns are silently filled with an empty string
The package runs fine either way, since mapping is purely cosmetic for documentation
questions.explain: You don't have to map every destination column — but if an unmapped column doesn't allow nulls, the load will fail at run time, because there's no value for it and no default the destination can fall back on. An unmapped nullable column simply loads as NULL, with no failure.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a Data Viewer, per Lesson 18.
options: It attaches to a path between two data flow components and pauses execution while showing the current buffer's rows
Clicking Detach stops the viewer from pausing execution, but data keeps flowing through the path at full speed
The green Continue arrow is always enabled, even when the entire data flow fits in a single buffer
A Data Viewer is meant to be left active on a package that's deployed to production, so you can keep monitoring it
Copy Data copies the current buffer's rows to the clipboard
questions.explain: A Data Viewer attaches to a path and pauses execution buffer by buffer, showing you the rows flowing through. Detach stops the pausing behavior while data keeps flowing at full speed. Copy Data copies the current buffer's rows to the clipboard. The Continue arrow is disabled, not always enabled, when the whole data flow fits in a single buffer, since there's nothing left to advance to. And a Data Viewer is strictly a development-time tool — leaving one active in a deployed, scheduled package makes it hang, waiting for a human who isn't there.

questions.prompt: A Lookup transformation is left at its default setting for rows that find no match in the reference dataset. What happens to an unmatched row by default?
options: It's treated as an error — you have to explicitly configure the Lookup to redirect rows to the No Match output instead
It's automatically redirected to the No Match output with no configuration needed
It's silently dropped from the data flow with no error and no redirect
It's passed through the Match output with the new lookup columns left NULL
questions.explain: By default, a row with no matching reference row is treated as an error. Getting unmatched rows onto their own separate path — a very common pattern for detecting "new" rows during an incremental load — requires explicitly setting the Lookup to redirect rows to no match output instead.

questions.prompt: A Conditional Split has two cases in this order: Case 1 tests FirstName starting with "A", Case 2 tests FirstName starting with "B". A row's FirstName is "Barbara". Which output does it go to, and why does order matter here?
options: Case 2 — conditions are evaluated top to bottom, and the row goes to the first case whose condition evaluates true; order only matters when a row could satisfy more than one case
Both Case 1 and Case 2, since Conditional Split sends a row down every case whose condition is true
The default output, because "Barbara" doesn't start with "A"
Case 1, because Conditional Split always evaluates cases in reverse order
questions.explain: Conditions in a Conditional Split are evaluated top to bottom, and as soon as one evaluates true, the row is sent there and every remaining condition is skipped for that row. "Barbara" doesn't match Case 1's "starts with A" test, so evaluation moves to Case 2, which it does match.

questions.prompt: A Derived Column transformation defines YearlyIncome as Replace 'YearlyIncome', using the expression REPLACENULL([YearlyIncome], 0) — and in the same transformation, a second derived column's expression also references [YearlyIncome]. Which value does that second expression actually see?
options: The original, pre-derived value of YearlyIncome — not the value this same transformation is about to write into it
The new, replaced value, since both expressions run in the same transformation and share state
NULL, because the column is mid-transformation and temporarily has no value
Whichever value was computed first, depending on the order the two rows appear in the grid
questions.explain: If an expression in a Derived Column transformation references a column that's being overwritten by that same transformation, the expression sees the original, pre-derived value, not the value about to be written. Chained transformations don't leak into each other mid-execution the way imperative code might suggest.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Aggregate transformation, per Lesson 23.
options: It is asynchronous — it has to consume the entire rowset before it can produce any output
It passes through every input column untouched, in addition to the grouped/aggregated columns
A single input column can have more than one aggregation applied to it, such as both Sum and Average
It supports Group By, Sum, Average, Count, Count distinct, Minimum, and Maximum — seven operations in total
Minimum and Maximum can be applied to any data type, including image and text columns
questions.explain: The Aggregate transformation is asynchronous, consuming the entire rowset before producing output, because a group's final value can't be known until every row in it has been seen. A single column can have multiple aggregations applied — Sum and Average on the same column, for instance. It supports exactly seven operations in total. It does not pass through untouched columns: only columns used for grouping or aggregation survive to the output. And Minimum/Maximum only work on numeric, date, or time types, not every data type.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 4 transformation to the one thing that makes it distinct from the others.
right: Converts a column's data type into a new output column — it doesn't reshape values with an expression
Routes each row to exactly one of several outputs based on which condition is the first to evaluate true
Required before Merge or Merge Join, because both require their inputs to already be sorted
Joins input columns against a reference dataset — a table, view, query, or cache file — to pull in related columns
questions.explain: Lookup joins against a reference dataset to pull in related columns, the way a SQL join would. Conditional Split routes each row to the first output whose condition evaluates true. Data Conversion exists purely to fix a type mismatch, copying a converted value into a new output column rather than applying an expression. Sort is the mandatory setup step Merge and Merge Join both depend on, since both require sorted input on their join/merge columns.

questions.prompt: A variable has EvaluateAsExpression set to True, with its Expression set to DATEPART("mm", GETDATE()). What does this variable actually hold?
options: The live result of that expression, recalculated every time the variable is evaluated — not a fixed value typed in once
The literal text string "DATEPART(\"mm\", GETDATE())", since EvaluateAsExpression only affects display formatting
Whatever value was last typed into the Value column before EvaluateAsExpression was turned on
NULL, because EvaluateAsExpression and a literal Value can't both be set on the same variable
questions.explain: Setting EvaluateAsExpression to True makes the variable recalculate its value from its Expression every time it's evaluated, instead of holding a fixed literal. A variable set this way to DATEPART("mm", GETDATE()) always holds the current month, live, not a value frozen at design time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inside an SSIS expression, a variable is referenced with an ________ sign, its namespace, and its name — for example, @[User::varFileName].
questions.explain: Every variable is referenced with an @ sign, its namespace (User:: or System::), and its name, written as @[Namespace::Name]. Parameters instead use $Package:: or $Project:: in place of the @ sign, matching their own scopes.

questions.prompt: Match each parameter concept to what it actually is, per Lesson 27.
right: Overrides the design default for every execution of the deployed project, set after deployment
Defined once in Project.params; usable by every package in the project
Set for one specific run only; overrides both the design and server values
Defined on one package's Parameters tab; usable only by that package
questions.explain: A project parameter is defined once in Project.params and usable by every package in the project. A package parameter is defined on one package's own Parameters tab, usable only there. The server value, set after deployment, overrides the design default for every execution unless something more specific is supplied. The execution value, set for one specific run only, overrides both the design and server values — but only for that single execution.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about package configurations versus parameters, per Lesson 30.
options: Under the Package Deployment Model, Microsoft recommends using configurations rather than parameters, because parameters aren't invoked at all under that model
The Project Deployment Model replaces configurations with parameters plus SSISDB environments
An environment reference is what decides which environment's values a deployed project's parameters resolve to — promoting from TEST to PROD can be a server-side change with no redeployment
XML configuration files are a feature of the Project Deployment Model, not the legacy Package Deployment Model
A package built with project parameters is guaranteed to run normally under the Package Deployment Model
questions.explain: Microsoft's own guidance is direct: use configurations under the Package Deployment Model, since parameters aren't invoked at all there. The Project Deployment Model replaces configurations with parameters and SSISDB environments. An environment reference — not the package itself — decides which environment's values apply, so promoting TEST to PROD can be purely a server-side change. XML configuration files are actually the legacy Package Deployment Model's pattern, not the Project Deployment Model's. And a package built with project parameters can outright fail to execute under the Package Deployment Model, the opposite of guaranteed.

questions.prompt: A Data Conversion transformation's Configure Error Output dialog is left at its defaults for every column. One row's value truncates when converted to a shorter output column. What happens?
options: The Data Flow task fails immediately — Fail Component is the default disposition for both Error and Truncation on every column
The row is automatically redirected to the error output, since truncation always defaults to Redirect Row
The row continues down the normal output with the value silently cut short
SSIS raises a warning but ignores it completely, continuing as if nothing happened
The entire package stops, but the current Data Flow task's already-processed rows are rolled back automatically
The transformation skips that one row, keeps every already-committed row, but doesn't fail the task
questions.explain: Opened fresh, the Configure Error Output dialog sets both the Error and Truncation dispositions to Fail Component on every column, by default. Since nothing was changed from that default, the truncated value causes the Data Flow task to fail immediately, rather than being redirected or silently ignored.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes Ignore Failure, and option B describes Redirect Row — both are real dispositions this dialog lets you choose, but neither is the one every column starts on. You have to deliberately change the default to get Ignore Failure's silent pass-through or Redirect Row's separate error path; left untouched, Fail Component is what actually runs.

questions.prompt: A task inside a Sequence container, which itself sits inside a package, raises an OnError event. Neither the task nor the Sequence container has an OnError handler of its own, but the package does. What happens?
options: The event bubbles up the hierarchy — task to Sequence container to package — and runs at the package-level OnError handler, since nothing closer to the task caught it
The event simply vanishes, since only the task's own handler could have caught it
The event runs at every level simultaneously — the task's, the container's, and the package's handlers all fire
The package-level handler can only catch events raised directly by the package itself, not by a task nested inside a container
questions.explain: An unhandled event doesn't just disappear — it bubbles up to the next container in the hierarchy: task, then its Sequence container, then the package. Since neither the task nor the container has its own OnError handler, the event escalates all the way to the package-level handler, which is exactly why one package-level OnError handler is often enough to catch failures anywhere in a package.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a package's CheckpointUsage property set to ________ restarts from the checkpoint file if it exists, and otherwise starts clean from the beginning — the setting used most often in practice.
questions.explain: CheckpointUsage has three settings: Never (always start from the beginning), Always (always restart from the checkpoint, failing if the file doesn't exist), and IfExists (restart from the checkpoint if the file is there, otherwise start clean) — IfExists is the one used most often.

questions.prompt: Match each common SSIS failure category to the Chapter 6 tool or signal that actually helps diagnose or contain it, per Lesson 35.
right: An OnError handler that checks preconditions, like whether an expected file has actually arrived, before the rest of the package runs
Logging with the Operator and SourceName categories turned on, to reveal which account actually ran the failing step
An error output redirecting the bad rows so the ErrorCode/ErrorColumn can be inspected, instead of failing the whole load
An OnError handler to alert immediately, plus checkpoints so retrying doesn't redo already-succeeded tasks
questions.explain: A connection failure calls for an OnError alert plus checkpoints, so a retry doesn't redo already-succeeded tasks. A data type mismatch is exactly what error outputs exist for — redirect the bad rows and inspect ErrorCode/ErrorColumn. A permission issue is diagnosed by turning on logging's Operator and SourceName categories, since the account that actually ran the package is rarely the one the developer tested with. A downstream/dependency failure calls for an OnError handler that checks preconditions, like whether a file has actually arrived, before letting the rest of the package run.

questions.prompt: A package reloads an entire fifty-million-row source table every single run, even though only a dozen rows actually changed since last night. What pattern fixes this, and how does it know which rows to pull?
options: An incremental load using a watermark — a saved value like the maximum modified-date processed last run — to extract only rows newer than that value
Running the Aggregate transformation first, since it collapses the row count before the load happens
Switching the OLE DB Destination to fast load mode, since that's what actually controls how many rows get extracted
Adding a Sort transformation before the source, since sorting automatically skips rows that haven't changed
questions.explain: An incremental (delta) load solves exactly this problem using the watermark pattern: a saved value, usually the maximum modified-date or identity value processed last run, lets the extract query pull only rows newer than that value instead of reloading the entire source every time.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Slowly Changing Dimension Transformation's attribute types, per Lesson 37.
options: A Fixed attribute's value should never change once set; the wizard can flag an incoming change to it as an error
A Changing attribute overwrites the old value with no history kept — the classic Type 1 behavior
A Historical attribute overwrites the old value in place, exactly like a Changing attribute
Marking a column as Historical attribute adds a Historical Attribute Options page later in the wizard, asking how to track that history
An inferred member is a placeholder dimension record created when a fact row references a key that doesn't exist yet
questions.explain: A Fixed attribute should never change, and the wizard can flag a change to it as an error. A Changing attribute is the classic Type 1 behavior — overwrite with no history. Marking a column Historical attribute adds a Historical Attribute Options page asking how to track that history. An inferred member is a minimal placeholder record created when a fact row references a dimension key that doesn't exist yet. A Historical attribute does not overwrite in place — it keeps the old value in an expired record and inserts a new current one, which is the whole point of Type 2 tracking.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Script Task's code reports success or failure back to the control flow by setting ________ to Success or Failure.
questions.explain: Every Script Task's code revolves around the Dts object, and Dts.TaskResult is specifically how it reports back: set to ScriptResults.Success or ScriptResults.Failure, that's what tells the control flow whether the task actually succeeded.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a master package running two dependent child packages in the order they actually happen.
items: The master package starts and reads shared setup values, like a batch ID, into package variables
The first Execute Package Task runs its child package, using Project Reference to find it in the same project
On the Parameter Bindings page, a parent variable is mapped to the child package's own parameter
Control returns to the master package once the child finishes, and its success or failure decides what the next precedence constraint allows
The second Execute Package Task runs its own child, only after the first child's precedence constraint allows it
questions.explain: A master package typically starts by reading shared setup values, then its first Execute Package Task runs a child via Project Reference, with any needed values mapped on Parameter Bindings. Control returns to the master once that child finishes, and only then — governed by the precedence constraint between the two Execute Package Tasks — does the second child run, exactly the sequential dependency this lesson describes.

questions.prompt: What is the SSISDB catalog, and what has to be enabled on the instance before it can be created?
options: A real database hosted inside the SQL Server Database Engine, implemented with CLR stored procedures — so CLR integration has to be enabled at the instance level before it can be created
A separate Windows service, installed alongside SQL Server Agent, that has to be started before packages can be scheduled
A folder on the file system that stores .dtsx files, requiring only that the Integration Services service be running
A feature of SSDT itself, created automatically the first time a project is built, with no server-side setup required
A SQL Server Agent job type that has to be enabled in msdb before any package can be deployed
A registry-based store that requires the legacy Package Deployment Model to be enabled first
questions.explain: The SSISDB catalog is a real database, named SSISDB, hosted inside an actual instance of the SQL Server Database Engine — not a separate service, not a special edition. Because the catalog is implemented with CLR stored procedures, CLR integration has to be enabled at the instance level before it can be created at all.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C mistakes the SSISDB catalog for a plain file-system folder of .dtsx files, and confuses it with the legacy Integration Services Windows service from Lesson 3 — which really is optional and unrelated to creating the catalog. SSISDB is a genuine SQL Server database with a purpose-built schema, and the one real instance-level prerequisite is CLR integration, not that legacy service being started.

questions.prompt: A project contains three packages. Under the project deployment model, how many separate deployments does it take to get all three packages onto the SSISDB catalog?
options: One — the whole project, including every package inside it and its parameters, builds into a single .ispac file that deploys as one unit
Three — each package has to be deployed individually, one .ispac per package
It depends on how many connection managers the project uses
None — packages in a project deployment model project run directly from SSDT with no deployment step at all
questions.explain: Under the project deployment model, an entire project — every package inside it, plus its parameters — is built into a single .ispac file, and that whole file deploys to the SSISDB catalog as one unit. You don't deploy packages individually; you deploy the project they live in.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a single package execution can reference only ________ SSISDB environment — never a mix of two at once.
questions.explain: A single package execution can reference only one environment. Even if a project has references to both Dev and Production, you pick exactly one of them when starting that execution — you can never mix variables from two environments in a single run.

questions.prompt: Match each scheduling/monitoring concept to what it actually controls, per Lessons 44 and 45.
left: Logging level set to Basic (the default)
right: Only appears when the job step's logging level was set to Performance or Verbose for that run
The identity a SQL Server Agent job step actually executes under, often different from the developer's own login
The job step setting pointing at a package deployed to SSISDB, matching the project deployment model
Means the Execution Performance report's Data Flow Components table comes back empty for that run
questions.explain: The Run as / proxy account is the identity the job step actually executes under, which is often not the developer's own login — the most common reason a package runs fine in SSDT but fails from a job. Logging level Basic means the Execution Performance report's Data Flow Components table comes back empty. Package Source: SSIS Catalog is the job step setting pointing at a deployed package. And the per-component Active Time/Total Time detail only appears when that run's logging level was Performance or Verbose.

questions.prompt: The capstone's dbo.CapstoneFactOrderSales table stores ProductKey, not the AdventureWorks2012 ProductID the source rows actually carry. Why?
options: ProductKey is the warehouse's own surrogate key, and the Lookup transformation has to resolve ProductID to it before a row can be written — there's no ProductKey to write until that lookup succeeds
ProductID can't be stored in AdventureWorksDW2014 because the two databases use incompatible data types for integers
Storing ProductKey instead of ProductID is purely a naming preference with no functional difference
ProductKey is generated by the OLE DB Destination automatically, with no Lookup transformation required
questions.explain: ProductKey is a warehouse-generated surrogate key standing in for the source system's business key, ProductID. The Lookup transformation is what resolves ProductID to its matching ProductKey in CapstoneDimProduct — there's simply no surrogate key value to write into the fact table until that lookup has already happened.

questions.prompt: In the capstone package, the Lookup transformation has to run before the OLE DB Destination, not after. Why specifically?
options: The destination table stores ProductKey, which only exists in the pipeline once the Lookup resolves it from ProductID — there's nothing to map into that destination column until the Lookup has already run
SSIS requires every Lookup to be the first component after the source, regardless of what the destination needs
Running the Lookup after the destination would cause the destination to insert duplicate rows
The Derived Column transformation can't compute DateKey unless the Lookup has already executed
questions.explain: CapstoneFactOrderSales stores ProductKey, not ProductID, and there's no surrogate key to write until the Lookup resolves one. The Derived Column transformation, by contrast, doesn't depend on the Lookup at all — its DateKey and ExtendedAmount expressions only reference OrderDate, OrderQty, and UnitPrice, which is exactly why Derived Column could run before or after the Lookup without breaking anything.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the changes Lesson 48 makes to the capstone package.
options: The Lookup's error-output setting changes from Fail Component to Redirect Row, so an unmatched ProductID lands in a CSV instead of silently disappearing
The OLE DB Destination's truncate step becomes more important than ever, since every run still needs to reload the whole fact table
An OnError event handler on the Data Flow Task inserts a row into a custom log table, so a failure leaves a record even if nobody was watching
The source query changes to filter on soh.ModifiedDate using a watermark, so only new or changed orders get extracted
Checkpoints are the one piece Lesson 48 says is strictly required, with no "optional" framing at all
questions.explain: Lesson 48 switches the Lookup's error output to Redirect Row so unmatched rows land in a CSV instead of disappearing, adds an OnError handler that logs failures to a custom table, and changes the source query to filter on ModifiedDate against a saved watermark. The truncate step is removed entirely once the load becomes incremental — every run only extracts what's new, so nothing needs reloading from scratch. And checkpoints are explicitly introduced as optional in this lesson, not a strict requirement.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the finished capstone package's incremental run in the order they actually execute, per Lesson 48.
items: An Execute SQL Task reads the last run's watermark from CapstoneLoadControl into a package variable
The OLE DB Source extracts only rows where ModifiedDate is newer than that watermark
The Lookup resolves ProductKey from ProductID, redirecting any unmatched row to an error file instead of failing
The Derived Column transformation computes DateKey and ExtendedAmount
The OLE DB Destination loads the fact table, redirecting any rejected row to its own error file
A final Execute SQL Task updates CapstoneLoadControl to the current run's time
questions.explain: The run starts by reading the saved watermark into a variable, then the source query uses it to extract only rows newer than that value. Inside the data flow, the Lookup resolves ProductKey (redirecting unmatched rows instead of failing), the Derived Column computes DateKey and ExtendedAmount, and the destination loads the fact table (redirecting its own rejected rows). Only after the data flow succeeds does a final Execute SQL Task update the watermark, so next run picks up exactly where this one left off.
